usage: native-Korean number, used for age, counting people/things
스물 → 스무 before a counter like 살
스물 → 스무 before the counter 명
examples: I'm twenty years old this year.
age uses 살; 스물 becomes 스무 before 살
개 counts objects; 스물 → 스무 before a counter
There are twenty students in the class.
명 counts people; note 스무 not 스물
nuance: 스물 is the native-Korean word for twenty and is the standard way to say someone's age in everyday speech. Like 하나·둘·셋·넷, it changes shape before a counter: 스물 becomes 스무 (스무 살, 스무 개, 스무 명). For higher ages and counting people or objects, Koreans use these native numbers, not the Sino-Korean 이십.
mistakes: Saying '스물 살' instead of '스무 살' before the counter
Using 스물 for things like phone numbers or dates, where Sino-Korean 이십 is needed

usage: native-Korean number, often used for age
examples: My older sister is thirty years old.
nuance: 서른 is the native-Korean number for thirty, used most often when telling age. Unlike 하나~넷, 서른 itself does not change shape, but the small number after it does (서른한, 서른두, 서른세, 서른네 살). For ages from twenty up, native numbers like 스물, 서른, 마흔 are the natural choice in conversation.
mistakes: Mixing it up with Sino-Korean 삼십 when saying age
Forgetting that the ones digit changes form, e.g. saying '서른둘 살' instead of '서른두 살'

examples: My dad is forty years old.
마흔이 넘다 = to be past forty
nuance: 마흔 is the native-Korean number for forty and is the usual word for a person's age in that range. The number itself stays the same, but a following ones digit shifts form (마흔한, 마흔두, 마흔세, 마흔네 살). Native numbers run 스물·서른·마흔·쉰 for the tens, which beginners use mostly for age and counting.
mistakes: Saying Sino-Korean 사십 for someone's age instead of 마흔
Mispronouncing it as '마은'; the ㅎ is written even if softly heard

examples: Grandma is over fifty years old.
넘다 = to exceed; 으셨 adds respect
nuance: 쉰 is the native-Korean number for fifty and is used to talk about age in daily life. It is short but spelled with a final ㄴ. As with the other tens, the ones digit added after it changes form (쉰한, 쉰두, 쉰세, 쉰네 살). For round ages like fifty, 쉰 sounds far more natural than the Sino-Korean 오십.
mistakes: Confusing 쉰 (fifty) with 쉬다 (to rest), which sound similar
Using 오십 for age when 쉰 is expected in conversation

examples: 다 되다 = to be nearly; 셨 adds respect
nuance: 예순 is the native-Korean number for sixty, used mainly for age. It is easy to confuse in sound with 여섯 (six), so listen for the full word. Like the other tens, a following ones digit changes shape (예순한, 예순두, 예순세, 예순네 살). For an older person's age, 예순 is the natural spoken choice over 육십.
mistakes: Mixing up 예순 (sixty) with 여섯 (six) because they sound alike
Saying 육십 for a person's age instead of native 예순

examples: 되다 = to become; 셨 adds respect
nuance: 일흔 is the native-Korean number for seventy and is the everyday word for that age. Beginners rarely need to count this high for objects, but it is common when talking about grandparents. The ones digit added after it shifts form (일흔한, 일흔두, 일흔세, 일흔네 살), just like the lower tens.
mistakes: Confusing it with 일곱 (seven) since both start with 일
Using Sino-Korean 칠십 for someone's age instead of 일흔

examples: My great-grandmother is eighty years old.
nuance: 여든 is the native-Korean number for eighty, used chiefly to describe age. It can sound close to 여덟 (eight) and 여섯 (six), so context matters. As with all the tens, a following ones digit changes form (여든한, 여든두, 여든세, 여든네 살). For an elder's age, 여든 is preferred over the Sino-Korean 팔십.
mistakes: Mixing up 여든 (eighty) with 여덟 (eight)
Saying 팔십 for a person's age where native 여든 is natural

examples: My great-grandfather is ninety years old.
nuance: 아흔 is the native-Korean number for ninety, used almost only for age. It is the last of the native tens (스물·서른·마흔·쉰·예순·일흔·여든·아흔), after which counting usually switches to Sino-Korean 백 for one hundred. The ones digit after it changes shape (아흔한, 아흔두, 아흔세, 아흔네 살).
mistakes: Confusing 아흔 (ninety) with 아홉 (nine) since both start with 아
Trying to say a hundred as a native number; 백 (Sino-Korean) is used instead

usage: the form of 하나 used before a counter word
개 is the general counter for objects
시 marks the hour; uses native numbers
examples: 명 is the counter for people
the hour uses native numbers, so 한 시
nuance: 한 is the special form of 하나 (one) used right before a counter such as 개, 명, 잔, or 시. Korean almost always puts a counter after a number, and 하나 changes to 한 in that position. The same shift happens with 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네, and 스물→스무.
mistakes: Saying '하나 개' instead of '한 개' before a counter
Forgetting a counter entirely, e.g. saying '커피 한' instead of '커피 한 잔'

usage: the form of 둘 used before a counter word
examples: I have class at two o'clock.
the hour uses native numbers, so 두 시
nuance: 두 is the form of 둘 (two) that appears before a counter like 개, 명, 병, or 시. Whenever a counter follows, 둘 becomes 두. This pre-counter change is shared by 하나→한, 셋→세, 넷→네, and 스물→스무, and beginners hear it constantly when ordering or telling time.
mistakes: Saying '둘 개' instead of '두 개' before a counter
Using Sino-Korean 이 for clock hours, e.g. '이 시' instead of '두 시'

usage: the form of 셋 used before a counter word
examples: the hour uses native numbers, so 세 시
nuance: 세 is the form of 셋 (three) used directly before a counter such as 개, 명, 잔, or 시. Korean numbers from one to four change shape before counters, so 셋 becomes 세. Remember the set 한·두·세·네 together, because these four forms come up in nearly every shopping or time-telling sentence.
mistakes: Saying '셋 개' instead of '세 개' before a counter
Using Sino-Korean 삼 for clock hours, e.g. '삼 시' instead of '세 시'

usage: the form of 스물 used before a counter word
스물 → 스무 before the counter 살
examples: 개 counts objects, not 스물 개
명 counts people; note 스무 not 스물
nuance: 스무 is the form of 스물 (twenty) used right before a counter such as 살, 개, or 명. Twenty is the one higher native number that still changes shape before a counter, joining 한·두·세·네. So you say 스무 살 and 스무 개, never 스물 살 or 스물 개, even though the plain number is 스물.
mistakes: Saying '스물 살' or '스물 개' instead of '스무 살' and '스무 개'
Forgetting that only 스물 (not 서른, 마흔...) also drops its final sound before a counter

usage: question word placed before a counter
literally 'how many o'clock,' uses native-number counters
examples: 몇 시 = what time, the most common use
How many people are in your family?
몇 + 명 to ask a number of people
Please give me a few apples.
here 몇 means 'a few,' not a question
nuance: 몇 means 'how many' and goes right before a counter, just like a number does (몇 개, 몇 명, 몇 시). It pairs with native-number counters and is essential for asking the time and quantities. The same word can also mean 'a few' (몇 개 = a few) when it is not a question.
mistakes: Using 몇 without a counter, e.g. saying '몇이에요?' instead of '몇 개예요?'
Confusing 몇 시 (what time, native numbers) with 며칠 (what date, Sino-Korean)

usage: the first one in order; also 'first of all'
the oldest child in a family
first day of a trip, class, etc.
the next ordinal after 첫째, for comparison
examples: common way to say birth order
On the first day of the trip, we went to the sea.
First of all, health is the most important.
nuance: 첫째 means 'the first' and is the native-Korean ordinal for number one, built from the idea of 하나. It names the first child in a family (첫째, 둘째, 셋째) and the first day or item in a sequence. It also works like 'first of all' when listing reasons, paired with 둘째 (secondly).
mistakes: Mixing up 첫째 (first, native ordinal) with Sino-Korean 일 번 (number one) in lists
Using 하나 to mean 'first'; ordinals use 첫째, 둘째, 셋째, not the plain numbers
